title: Front doors
summary: Every way into the planner: the Rust library, the ff CLI, an MCP server for agents, Python and WASM bindings, a Bevy GUI, and a Claude skill. All are thin; all end in the same few library calls.
body:
ferroplan has one engine and seven ways in. The library crate exposes solve, parse, decompose, validate_plan, trace, the classic-text run_ff/run_planner, and the stateful Session. Every other crate in this section is a translation layer: it turns its own input convention (argv, JSON-RPC, Python args, JS values, Bevy keypresses) into an Options plus two PDDL strings, calls the library, and serializes the Solution it gets back, usually as the same JSON.

Two design choices recur. First, JSON as the lingua franca: CLI --json, MCP, Python and WASM all emit the serde form of Solution, so tooling written against one works against all. Second, keep the search off the UI thread: MCP uses spawn_blocking, the web demo a Web Worker, the GUI Bevy's async task pool.

children.title: Rust library API
children.summary: The crate's public surface: solve, parse, decompose, validate_plan, trace, run_ff/run_planner and Session. Every other front door is a thin wrapper over these.
children.body:
Every front door in this section ends at a handful of functions re-exported from crates/ferroplan/src/lib.rs. The library is the product; the CLI, MCP server, Python wheel, WASM module and Bevy GUI only translate their own input conventions into an Options struct and a pair of PDDL source strings, then serialize what comes back.

  • solve(domain, problem, &Options) -> Result<Solution, SolveError> (api.rs:597): parse, ground, route by Mode (Auto picks temporal for durative domains, PDDL3 for preferences, else classical FF) and return a typed, serde-serializable Solution { solved, mode, plan, statistics, notes }.
  • parse(src) -> ParseReport (api.rs:341): syntax-check a domain or problem without grounding. Used by the MCP parse tool.
  • decompose(...) (api.rs:952): split a too-big temporal goal into ordered contracts and stitch them.
  • plan::validate_plan (plan.rs:125): replay a plan under ferroplan's own semantics.
  • run_ff / run_planner (planner.rs:700, :15): the classic-text renderers that return (String, exit_code), kept so ff stays a Metric-FF drop-in.
  • trace(domain, problem, &steps) (trace.rs:26): replay a plan into per-step StateSnapshots; the GUI animator's input.
  • Session, Think, ThinkBudget, ThinkVerdict (lib.rs:101): the ground-once embedding API (next section).

The schema cargo feature gives Options/Mode/Search a JsonSchema derive; the MCP server turns it on so tool inputs advertise real knobs.

children.title: Call paths into the core
children.summary: One table: which function each front door calls, with which Options, on which thread.
children.body:

The pattern is the same everywhere: strings in, a serde Solution out. Nothing outside crates/ferroplan touches grounding or search internals. The GUI is the one exception that reaches deeper, into the parser's types::Domain AST, because its block editor edits that AST directly.

children.title: ff CLI (ferroplan-cli)
children.summary: The `ff` binary: a Metric-FF drop-in (`ff -o domain -f problem`) plus JSON, validate and decompose modes. 302 lines, all translation.
children.body:
A 302-line crate whose job is to make ferroplan a drop-in for Metric-FF's command line while exposing the library's extras. It parses flags with clap, builds an Options, and calls exactly one of five library entry points depending on flags. It owns no planning logic.

Call path: main → Cli::to_options → run_planner | run_ff | solve | decompose | plan::validate_plan → print. Build with cargo build --release -p ferroplan-cli; binary is target/release/ff.

children.title: Flags to Options
children.summary: clap derive struct Cli; to_options() maps flags 1:1 onto ferroplan::Options. The per-call wall/cancel fields are deliberately left None.
children.body:
struct Cli (main.rs:81) is a clap derive. The Metric-FF-compatible core is -o/--domain and -f/--problem; everything else is a ferroplan extension: --json, --json-request FILE|-, --mode (auto, ff, partition, pddl3, temporal, portfolio, optimal, sat), --search (auto, ehc, best-first, ehc-then-best-first), --no-helpful, --weight-g (default 1.0), --weight-h (default 5.0), --max-evaluated, --satisfice, --threads (0 = auto), --ipc, --validate PLAN, --decompose.

Cli::to_options (main.rs:146) builds an Options literal: helpful_actions = !no_helpful, optimize = !satisfice. Two fields stay None on purpose: wall_ms and should_continue. The comment explains why: ff is one process running one call, which is the shape the process-wide FF_TIME_LIMIT env var already fits. The per-call budget exists for long-lived hosts that solve on many threads and need to bound or withdraw one of them.

ModeArg and SearchArg are local ValueEnums with From impls into the library's Mode and Search, so the CLI's spelling (kebab-case) is decoupled from the library enum.

children.title: main(): dispatch order
children.summary: main() checks, in order: --json-request, then -o/-f with --validate, --decompose, --json, else classic text via run_planner / run_ff.
children.body:
main (main.rs:238) is a short priority chain:

  1. JSON job. --json-request reads a JobRequest { domain, problem, options } (PDDL as strings, options any subset thanks to serde defaults) from a file or stdin, calls ferroplan::solve, prints pretty JSON, exits 0 if solved else 1.
  2. Files. Otherwise both -o and -f are required.
  3. Validate. --validate calls plan::validate_plan and prints Plan valid / Plan invalid: reason (exit 0/1). No solving.
  4. Decompose. --decompose calls ferroplan::decompose and prints either JSON or render_decomposition's human view: each contract's goal, offset, timed steps and makespan, then the stitched plan.
  5. JSON solve. --json calls solve.
  6. Classic text. --mode ff goes to run_ff (plain FF best-first, the engine mode); every other mode goes to run_planner, the SGPlan-style partition-and-resolve meta-planner that also handles routing to PDDL3, temporal and SAT text output.

The text paths do not go through solve: they return (String, i32) already formatted, which is how the exit-code and message contract of Metric-FF is preserved byte for byte for the differential test harness.

children.title: Output: FF text, IPC, JSON
children.summary: Three output shapes: Metric-FF classic text (default), IPC time-stamped (--ipc), and the structured Solution JSON.
children.body:
Classic FF text mimics Metric-FF: progress lines like ff: parsing domain file, then step N: ACTION ARGS lines. Action names come out upper-cased (PICK R1 B1) because the grounder interns upper-case displays; the authoring skill warns about this. Exit code follows Metric-FF's contract, so scripts written for ff keep working.

IPC (--ipc, text mode only) renders the time-stamped form t: (action args) [dur] that IPC validators and VAL read.

JSON (--json or --json-request) prints the library's Solution directly: plan.steps[] with index, action, args, optional time/duration, plus metric, makespan, statistics and free-form notes (e.g. why EHC fell back). This is the same JSON the MCP solve tool, the Python plan() and the WASM plan() return, so one parser handles every front door.

children.title: MCP server (ferroplan-mcp)
children.summary: A Model Context Protocol server over stdio exposing four one-shot planning tools and a ten-tool stateful Session surface to an LLM agent.
children.body:
The MCP server makes the project's thesis operational: the agent writes and supervises PDDL, the planner runs deterministically. It has two shapes. One-shot: solve, parse, validate, decompose, each taking the PDDL it needs. Stateful: session_*, which grounds a world once and then takes incremental updates and rethinks, the shape a running simulation actually has. session_fork gives each actor its own mind over one shared grounded world.

Call path: agent JSON-RPC → rmcp router → Ferroplan::<tool> → ferroplan::solve / Session method (on spawn_blocking when it grounds or searches) → pretty JSON text block.

children.title: rmcp over stdio
children.summary: Built on rmcp, the official MCP Rust SDK. Tool schemas are derived from parameter types; stdout is the protocol, so diagnostics go to stderr.
children.body:
main.rs is 33 lines: server::Ferroplan::new().serve(stdio()).await on a tokio runtime. All protocol details (framing, capability negotiation, tool listing, error conventions) come from rmcp via the #[tool_router], #[tool] and #[tool_handler] macros rather than a hand-rolled loop.

Tool input schemas are derived with schemars::JsonSchema on structs like SolveArgs { domain, problem, options: Option<Options> }. That is why the crate depends on ferroplan with features = ["schema"]: the agent sees Options' actual fields, not an opaque object.

Errors are split deliberately. A request that routed fine but could not be done (bad PDDL, unknown session) returns CallToolResult::error, visible to the agent so it can fix its input. Only internal failures (a panicked blocking task) become protocol ErrorData. Results are pretty JSON in a text block, kept identical to the pre-rmcp server so older prompts still parse.

The #[tool_handler] instructions string tells the agent the two usage shapes: one-shot solve, or session_open then a tell/replan loop.

children.title: Stateless tools (solve, parse, ...)
children.summary: Four one-shot tools, each taking the PDDL it needs. solve and decompose run on spawn_blocking; parse and validate are synchronous.
children.body:
• solve (server.rs:228): SolveArgs → ferroplan::solve inside tokio::task::spawn_blocking. A solved: false result is a normal answer, not an error.
  • parse (:252): ferroplan::parse(pddl), auto-detecting domain vs problem; returns ok/error with a line number plus name, requirements and counts, so an agent can syntax-check while authoring without paying for grounding.
  • validate (:263): plan::validate_plan; returns Plan valid or Plan invalid: why.
  • decompose (:280): ferroplan::decompose on a blocking thread; returns contracts and the stitched plan.

These embody the README's bet: the LLM authors and supervises PDDL, the planner runs deterministically. Keeping parse separate from solve lets the agent iterate on syntax cheaply before asking for a search.

children.title: Session tools (session_*)
children.summary: Ten tools over ferroplan::Session: open, close, list, fork, set, observe, elapse, apply_start, replan, state. The world grounds once per session_open.
children.body:
The server keeps sessions: Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, Session>>> and hands out ids s1, s2, ... from an AtomicU64. A compile-time assertion checks Session: Send + Sync next to the map that depends on it.

  • session_open: Session::new on spawn_blocking (grounding is the expensive part); returns goal_met, world_bytes, mind_bytes.
  • session_set: facts, then fluents, then timed facts, then goal, in that order, stopping at the first rejection and reporting how many of each applied. Fences (static facts, RUNNING-* tokens) are refused by name.
  • session_observe: Session::observe, returning the surprises.
  • session_elapse / session_apply_start: the temporal clock.
  • session_fork: Session::fork, the many-minds primitive; reports the fork's mind_bytes.
  • session_replan: Session::think with a ThinkBudget built from max_evaluated, wall_ms, memory_mb.
  • session_state, session_list, session_close: read-back and housekeeping. Handles do not survive a server restart and the error says so.

children.title: Locking: fork, drop lock, think
children.summary: Cheap mutations run under the map lock; session_replan forks the mind under the lock, releases it, and searches on a blocking thread so one deep search never freezes other sessions.
children.body:
with_session (server.rs:207) takes the std::sync::Mutex, looks up the id, runs a closure, and releases. A poisoned mutex is recovered with into_inner() on the grounds that the map is still readable state. This path is used only for cheap calls: set, observe, elapse, apply_start, state.

session_replan (:550) is the long pole and does something specific: inside one spawn_blocking it locks, calls s.fork(), and drops the guard. A second spawn_blocking then runs mind.think(&budget) with no lock held. Because fork shares the grounded payload behind Arc and copies only the small per-mind state (see Session: fork), this snapshot is cheap, and a long search cannot stall the tokio runtime or every other session on the server. The lock is never held across an .await.

A consequence worth knowing: replan works on a snapshot, so it does not mutate the stored session. That fits the API, since think takes &self anyway.

children.title: Budget-stamped replan on the wire
children.summary: session_replan returns the usual Solution JSON plus four additive fields: capped, spent_ms, spent_evals, verdict.
children.body:
Since 0.24 the replan payload is the Solution serialized exactly as before, with capped, spent_ms, spent_evals and verdict (solved | capped | exhausted, kebab-case from ThinkVerdict) written alongside. The stamp is additive so standing agent prompts keep parsing.

The contract for an agent: capped never means unsolvable. Only a classical complete search that ran out of states reads exhausted; temporal thinks never claim a proof. The tests a_capped_think_never_reads_unsolvable_on_the_wire and an_orbit_aware_replan_narrates_itself pin this at the protocol level.

The code comment names a seam: when the SAT mode lands for sessions, mode in this same payload would read "sat", with no new tool and no new field.

children.title: Python bindings (ferroplan-py)
children.summary: pyo3 bindings built with maturin: one plan() call that returns Solution JSON. One-shot only; no Session in Python.
children.body: The smallest front door. Call path: Python ferroplan.plan(d, p, mode, threads) → pyo3 trampoline → ferroplan_core::solve on the calling thread → serde_json::to_string → Python str. The GIL is held for the whole solve (the binding does not release it), so concurrent Python threads serialize on it; ferroplan's own data-parallel pool still uses multiple cores inside the call.

children.title: ferroplan.plan() and version()
children.summary: Two pyfunctions. plan(domain, problem, mode=None, threads=None) returns the Solution as a JSON string, or {"error": ...}.
children.body:
plan (lib.rs:23) builds Options { mode, ..Default }, optionally sets threads, calls ferroplan_core::solve, and returns serde_json::to_string(&sol). Errors are returned as a JSON string {"error": "..."} rather than raised as Python exceptions, so the Python side always does json.loads and checks a key.

parse_mode accepts ff, pddl3, partition, temporal; anything else (including None) is Auto. There is no Session binding in Python today: the surface is one-shot only.

import ferroplan, json
sol = json.loads(ferroplan.plan(domain_pddl, problem_pddl))
print(sol["solved"], sol["plan"]["length"])

Returning JSON strings instead of building Python objects keeps the binding at 64 lines and makes the payload byte-identical to the CLI's --json, MCP and WASM outputs.

children.title: maturin build, abi3 wheel
children.summary: Standalone workspace built by maturin, not cargo; abi3-py38 gives one wheel for Python 3.8+. The core crate is aliased ferroplan_core to free the name ferroplan for the module.
children.body:
crates/ferroplan-py/Cargo.toml declares its own empty [workspace] and the root workspace lists it under exclude. The reason is in the comment: pyo3's extension-module feature does not link libpython, so a plain cargo build of the workspace would fail to link. maturin (maturin develop / maturin build --release, configured in pyproject.toml) is the build tool.

The cdylib is named ferroplan so Python imports ferroplan; to avoid a crate-name clash the planner is depended on as ferroplan_core = { package = "ferroplan", path = "../ferroplan" }. pyo3 0.29 with abi3-py38 targets Python's stable ABI, so one wheel serves 3.8 onward (3.14 with PYO3_USE_ABI3_FORWARD_COMPATIBILITY=1).

Release coupling: CLAUDE.md's pre-flight lists "ferroplan-py version + re-lock" and the maturin wheel build, because this crate's version (0.30.0) is pinned by hand and its lockfile is separate from the workspace's.

children.title: WASM bindings (ferroplan-wasm)
children.summary: wasm-bindgen bindings that run the planner in the browser: one-shot plan()/explain() and a WasmSession class, plus the web/ demo that uses them.
children.body:
Call paths: Solver page → worker.js → plan() → features::set_overrides + ferroplan::solve (threads=1) → JSON string. Live pages → new WasmSession → Session::new, then per tick fork / think (→ replan_budgeted) / valid (→ plan_still_valid) / apply_start / elapse.

The crate type is ["cdylib", "rlib"]; the rlib lets smoke.js and Rust tests exercise the same code.

children.title: plan(), explain(), version()
children.summary: wasm_bindgen exports: plan() solves with threads=1 and per-call feature flags; explain() returns plan introspection JSON.
children.body:
plan(domain, problem, mode, flags, search) (lib.rs:27) always sets threads: 1. WASM has no threads here, and the library's data-parallel map falls back to a sequential pass that produces an identical result, so determinism carries over to the browser.

flags is a comma list of the planner's env-gated switches (tdemand, tdecomp, tconc). In native builds those are env vars; on wasm reading env vars panics, so apply_flags (:52) calls ferroplan::features::set_overrides(tdemand, tdecomp, tconc), an in-process override, and resets the whole managed set every call so one pick cannot leak into the next solve.

explain(domain, problem, plan_json) (:78) deserializes a Plan and calls introspect::explain: causal links for classical plans, invariant spans for temporal ones, preference breakdown for PDDL3. The demo shows it as an Explain panel under the plan.

Build (build.sh): cargo build -p ferroplan-wasm --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, then wasm-bindgen --target web --out-dir web/pkg. The wasm-bindgen crate is pinned =0.2.126 to match the installed CLI exactly.

children.title: WasmSession: minds in the browser
children.summary: A wasm_bindgen struct wrapping ferroplan::Session plus the mind's current plan and cursor, so the JS tick loop mirrors the native bazaar_live / village_live examples.
children.body:
WasmSession { inner: Session, plan: Option<Plan>, cursor } (lib.rs:123). The constructor grounds with threads: 1 and installs a panic hook that forwards to console.error. Methods map onto Session nearly 1:1: fork, set_goal, set_fact, set_fluent, set_timed_fact, observe (JSON in, surprises out), apply_start, elapse, goal_met, fact, fluent, world_bytes, mind_bytes.

Additions that live only here:

  • think(evals, mem_mb) calls replan_budgeted (not the stamped think), stores the plan, resets the cursor and returns the Solution JSON.
  • valid() is plan_still_valid(plan, cursor), the free suffix replay; step_json, suffix_json, advance, drop_plan walk the stored plan.
  • restrict_prefix_claims(prefix, claimed): the bazaar's actor scoping ("TRADE ALICE ") plus the claims policy, masking any op whose fifth token, the item received, is claimed by a rival.
  • restrict_contains(filter): the village's scoping (" BOB").
  • plan_valid_json(plan, from): validity of an arbitrary plan against this session, used by the village's probe pattern (fork the world, set the worker's contract, ask).

children.title: web/ demo site
children.summary: The static, server-less demo: Solver page, two live Session pages, a generated example corpus, a Web Worker and an opt-in offline service worker.
children.body: Everything runs client-side; nothing leaves the visitor's machine. The site is published under /demo/ on the project's Pages site and works from a plain python3 -m http.server checkout too (where BUILD reads dev).

children.title: Solver page + worker.js
children.summary: index.html imports the wasm module, sends solves to a module Web Worker so the page never freezes, and falls back to a synchronous in-page solve when workers are unavailable.
children.body:
web/index.html imports init, { plan, explain, version } from ./pkg/ferroplan_wasm.js and the example corpus from examples.js. A solve goes through solveWorker (index.html:398): it lazily creates new Worker('./worker.js', { type: 'module' }) and posts { id, domain, problem, mode, flags, search }.

worker.js (18 lines) awaits init() once, calls plan(...) and posts { id, res } back. Running off the main thread matters for two reasons: a heavy solve does not freeze the UI, and it can be cancelled by terminating and recreating the worker (wasm cannot be interrupted mid-call otherwise).

If the worker cannot be created (file:// origin, strict CSP) makeWorker marks it broken and the page calls plan() synchronously in the page; a "run on" toggle exposes this choice. After a solve the page offers Explain (calls explain) and Animate: it writes {domain, problem, solution, mode, search, at} to localStorage['ferroplan.handoff'] and navigates to ../gui/index.html#animate, where the Bevy GUI picks it up.

children.title: examples.js: the demo corpus
children.summary: An auto-generated ES module exporting DOMAINS: each entry a key, label, note, the domain PDDL and graded problems, for the two-level picker.
children.body:
examples.js is generated (its first line says so) and exports DOMAINS, an array of objects with key, label, note, domain and a set of graded problems. It is 21 physical lines but large, because each line embeds full PDDL.

The corpus walks the feature ladder: gripper (STRIPS), fuel and travel (numeric), courier (ADL forall + when), reachable regions (derived axioms), loot (PDDL3 preferences), logistics, job shop, overlapping work (temporal), villagers, rpg-world (durative crafting and the decomposer, with notes about which in-browser flags each grade needs), log cabin and its crew/skilled-crew/forge-order variants (makespan vs crew size), elevators with action costs and net benefit (IPC-2008), barman (the LAMA rung) and bazaar-chain (the game track).

Several notes are teaching text: logistics states its border ("only solves the single-package / single-vehicle shape"), barman warns of roughly half a minute in the browser. bazaar-live.html also imports DOMAINS to fetch the bazaar fixture rather than duplicating it.

children.title: sw.js: opt-in offline copy
children.summary: A service worker registered only when the visitor clicks Save offline; precaches the three pages, corpus and wasm bundle, then serves stale-while-revalidate.
children.body:
Inert until asked: the page registers ./sw.js only from the Save offline button (index.html:637). On install it precaches the SHELL list: index.html, examples.js, worker.js, village-live.html, village-data.js, bazaar-live.html, manifest, icon, pkg/ferroplan_wasm.js and pkg/ferroplan_wasm_bg.wasm.

Versioning. The cache name is ferroplan-demo- + BUILD, where __BUILD_ID__ is replaced by the Pages workflow with the deploying commit. A new deploy installs alongside the old cache and activate deletes every other ferroplan-demo-* cache, so the offline site is always one whole build, never a mix.

Fetch. Same-origin GETs only: answer from cache (with ignoreSearch) and refresh in the background (stale-while-revalidate); on a miss go to network; offline and uncached, a navigation falls back to index.html, anything else gets an honest 503. Cross-origin requests (Google Fonts) pass through untouched because opaque responses cannot be inspected.

A message handler answers {type:'status'} over a MessagePort with build id, file count and total cached bytes, which the button displays.

children.title: village-live / bazaar-live pages
children.summary: Two pages that run real Session tick loops client-side via WasmSession: a temporal village of workers and a multi-mind barter bazaar.
children.body:
village-live.html creates one WasmSession(VILLAGE_DOMAIN, VILLAGE_PROBLEM) as the authoritative world. Per worker per tick, workerTurn: fork a probe, set_goal the worker's contract and test goal_met; if not done, check plan_valid_json on the worker's plan from its cursor; if broken, think on a fresh fork scoped with restrict_contains(w.filter); then dispatch due steps with world.apply_start. The world then elapses, firing interval ends. It is the same loop as examples/village_live.rs.

bazaar-live.html replays the many-minds barter run: each mind is a fork scoped with restrict_prefix_claims, follows its plan while valid() holds, counts a conflict when a rival's trade broke it, and re-thinks with a bounded think(THINK_EVALS, THINK_MB).

Both run on the main thread (no worker) because each think is budgeted small. They show that the Session API is the same in the browser as natively: one grounding, many cheap forks, free validity replays.

children.title: GUI (ferroplan-bevy)
children.summary: A Bevy app that draws a problem as a typed graph, solves it off-thread, animates the plan (or a Gantt for temporal plans), and edits problems and domains as blocks. Native or in-browser.
children.body: The GUI keeps logic out of the view: graph construction and PDDL regeneration live in ferroplan::viz, state replay in ferroplan::trace, and the GUI is ECS systems over those results. Call paths: load → parser::parse_domain/parse_problem → VizGraph::build; S → AsyncComputeTaskPool → ferroplan::solve(Options::default()) → ferroplan::trace → tween; editor Apply → viz::to_pddl → Scene::load_src; browser startup → webhandoff::try_load.

children.title: main.rs: app, resources, build
children.summary: Registers resources and systems with Bevy; runs natively (window) or in the browser (canvas #ferroplan-canvas) from one codebase with a slimmed Bevy feature set.
children.body:
main (main.rs:19) adds DefaultPlugins with a 1280x820 window; on wasm32 it targets <canvas id="ferroplan-canvas">, fits it to the parent and keeps key/scroll events on the canvas. Resources: Scene, Selected, DragState, anim::Plan, SolveJob, blocks::Editor, blocks::Drag, Transport, GanttState. Startup systems set up camera, UI, transport, Gantt and startup_load; two Update tuples hold the per-frame systems.

Bevy 0.19 is pulled with default-features = false and only 2D rendering, sprites, text, UI, gizmos, assets, default font, webgl2, x11 and multi-threading, explicitly to shrink the wasm GUI (no audio, glTF, 3D, scenes, animation). build-wasm.sh builds with RUSTFLAGS='--cfg getrandom_backend="wasm_js"' because two getrandom versions are in the tree. Colors come from palette.rs, shared with the web redesign tokens; icons in icons.rs are procedural meshes so there is no art to license.

children.title: scene.rs: problem as a graph
children.summary: Loads PDDL (drag-drop, CLI args, editor, handoff), builds viz::VizGraph, spawns nodes and mobiles as entities, draws edges as gizmos, and pans/zooms the camera.
children.body:
Scene (scene.rs:24) is a Bevy resource holding the parsed Domain/Problem, their sources, the derived VizGraph, a dirty flag and a status string. load_src content-sniffs whether a string is a problem or domain (which of (PROBLEM/(DOMAIN appears first), parses with ferroplan::parser, and once both halves exist calls VizGraph::build(d, p).

The graph logic lives in the core crate's viz module, which is view-agnostic: static objects become nodes, static binary predicates (e.g. road) become edges, objects that move become mobiles placed on the node they are at.

Systems: handle_drops reads dropped .pddl files; respawn_graph despawns and respawns everything when dirty, laying nodes on a circle (radius grows with node count) and fanning mobiles on their node, each with a per-type mesh icon from icons.rs; draw_edges draws gizmo lines and highlights edges active in the current plan step; camera_nav handles right-drag pan and scroll zoom.

children.title: interact.rs + ui.rs: select and inspect
children.summary: Left-click selects a node or mobile, left-drag moves a node, a cyan gizmo ring marks the selection; ui.rs's side panel lists the selection's facts and the goal.
children.body:
interact (interact.rs:22) converts the cursor to world coordinates with viewport_to_world_2d, hit-tests nodes (radius NODE_SIZE*0.6) then mobiles, and writes the hit object name into the Selected resource. Holding the button drags the hit node by rewriting its Transform. The system yields entirely while the block editor is open or the transport bar is being scrubbed, so the pointer has one owner at a time.

draw_selection draws a ring with palette::CY (the design's "selected" cyan) around the selected entity.

ui::update_info rebuilds the side panel text each frame: scene status (or a drag-drop hint), the current plan status and step, and for the selected object every current fact that mentions it plus the goal. This is the inspector in the book's screenshots.

children.title: anim.rs: solve off-thread, tween
children.summary: S spawns ferroplan::solve on Bevy's AsyncComputeTaskPool; the result is replayed with ferroplan::trace into snapshots, and mobiles are eased between snapshot positions.
children.body:
controls (anim.rs:70): on S, if no job is running and both sources exist, it spawns solve_blocking(domain, problem) on AsyncComputeTaskPool. solve_blocking calls ferroplan::solve(&d, &p, &Options::default()), the same entry as the CLI's --json. poll_solve polls the task each frame with future::poll_once and hands the result to load_result.

result_from_solution (:166) turns a Solution into a SolveResult. For non-temporal plans it calls ferroplan::trace(domain, problem, &(action,args) pairs) to get a StateSnapshot per step. Temporal plans get no snapshots (overlapping actions cannot be tweened as a sequence) and are shown in the Gantt view instead.

The timeline cursor Plan.t is a step index for classical plans and plan time for temporal ones. advance moves it: classical at 1.5 steps per second scaled by each step's duration; temporal so the whole makespan plays in about 7 seconds. animate looks up each mobile's node in snapshots k and k+1 via VizGraph::positions_at and lerps with ease-in-out-cubic. Space plays/pauses, arrows step between marks (every start and, temporally, end), R resets.

children.title: gantt.rs + transport.rs: timeline views
children.summary: Temporal plans render as a Gantt chart with greedy lane packing and a cyan now-line; a bottom transport bar gives play/pause, a scrubbable track with one notch per step, and a readout.
children.body:
gantt.rs exists because a temporal plan's overlapping durative actions cannot be shown by moving mobiles one step at a time. pack_lanes (gantt.rs:133) sorts steps by start time and puts each in the first lane whose last action has ended (a greedy interval-partitioning pass, which is optimal in lane count for intervals sorted by start). rebuild_gantt respawns bars when the plan changes; gantt_now moves the now-line with Plan.t. Shown automatically for temporal plans, toggled with T.

transport.rs is the mouse-only mirror of the keyboard controls: a play button, a track that maps the pointer's RelativeCursorPosition to a timeline t on press or drag, notches at Plan::start_frac per step, a molten progress fill and a step/time readout. While the pointer is over it, Transport.hovering makes interact stand down.

children.title: blocks.rs: Blockly-style editor
children.summary: The largest file (1,771 lines): a click-and-drag block editor for problems (objects, init, goal) and domains (types, predicates, actions), regenerating PDDL with viz::to_pddl / domain_to_pddl.
children.body:
The editor is seeded from the loaded Scene: seed and seed_domain flatten the parsed AST (types::Action, Formula, Effect) into editable rows. Actions whose preconditions or effects do not flatten to literal lists plus when blocks keep their raw text. bevy_ui has no dropdown widget, so each field is a button that cycles through valid choices on click: type, predicate, or a type-compatible object (compatible_objects honors the type hierarchy via is_subtype).

apply_changes (blocks.rs:1057) regenerates the domain with viz::domain_to_pddl and the problem with viz::to_pddl and feeds both through Scene::load_src, so the graph re-renders from the same parser the planner uses. export_changes writes them to /tmp/<name>.pddl.

Keys: E toggles the editor, Tab switches problem/domain. While a text field has focus, anim::controls ignores keys so typing an S does not start a solve. Tests at the bottom of the file round-trip regenerated domains through ferroplan::parser::parse_domain.

children.title: webhandoff.rs: Animate this plan
children.summary: wasm32-only: at startup read localStorage['ferroplan.handoff'] written by the Solver page, load its domain/problem and its already-solved Solution, and autoplay.
children.body:
try_load (webhandoff.rs:19) reads the key via web_sys, parses JSON, requires domain and problem strings, and loads both into the Scene. If a solution field deserializes as ferroplan::Solution, it goes through the same anim::result_from_solution + load_result(..., autoplay=true) path as a native solve.

The design choice is to animate the plan the Solver page already found instead of re-solving: if search options ever differ between the two pages, re-solving could show a different plan from the one the user clicked on. A handoff without a solution still counts as loaded (the user can press S). If there is no handoff, main::startup_load falls back to the embedded demo/domain.pddl + demo/problem.pddl.

Natively, startup_load instead reads file paths from std::env::args.

children.title: .claude skill: ferroplan
children.summary: A Claude Code skill (.claude/skills/ferroplan) that teaches an agent to author, run and debug PDDL for this planner, with six verified minimal examples.
children.body: The skill is a front door for agents rather than programs. Its frontmatter triggers it when writing or fixing PDDL for ferroplan, choosing features, invoking ff or the library, interpreting plans, or decomposing a big goal. It contains SKILL.md (109 lines), reference.md (92 lines) and six example directories. Its call path into the core is the CLI: the agent runs ff -o ... -f ... (or --json, --validate, --decompose) and reads the output. The MCP server offers the same operations as tools for agents that are not in a shell.

children.title: The authoring loop + feature table
children.summary: Pick the smallest feature set, write, run ff, read the output, localize failures, never hand over PDDL that has not been run.
children.body:
The skill's core rule: author a domain, run it, and confirm a real plan comes out. Its rationale is stated plainly: models are fluent in Python but shaky in PDDL, and the cure is a run loop plus verified examples.

The feature table maps situations to requirements and to a minimal verified example under .claude/skills/ferroplan/examples/: strips-typing, numeric, adl, axioms (use :adl, not :derived-predicates), preferences (needs a (:metric minimize (is-violated p)) or the preference is ignored), temporal (--mode temporal). reference.md lists the remaining flags.

It also documents --validate as a self-check under ferroplan's own semantics, distinct from external VAL (which imposes strict PDDL2.1 concurrent-numeric mutex).

children.title: Engine gotchas + decomposition rule
children.summary: Verified quirks (upper-cased output, static-only axioms, explicit requirement tokens) and the measured border past which a goal must be split into contracts.
children.body:
• Output is upper-cased; match plan steps case-insensitively.
  • (when ...) without :conditional-effects is a parse error, not silently dropped; likewise :universal-preconditions for forall and :negative-preconditions for not.
  • Axioms are static-only: the derived closure is computed once into init and the rules cleared; a :derived body reading an action-changed predicate errors.
  • Temporal: simultaneous starts are epsilon-separated (a start at 3.001 keeps an over-all condition strictly inside).
  • Empty types ground to zero instances rather than failing.

Decomposition. The measured rule quoted from examples/BORDERS.md: the delete-relaxed heuristic keeps a gradient on linear or accumulative work and goes flat the instant two or more contributions must converge on one goal quantity. Hand a contract whole if it is one accumulating chain (up to about 2000 ops) or every goal quantity gets at most one converging contribution; otherwise split, or let ff --decompose do it.

title: Session: ground once, think forever
summary: The embedding API for callers that re-solve the same world every tick: ground once, mutate the live state, and pay only search per think, with cheap forks for many minds.
body:
This section covers crates/ferroplan/src/session.rs. The core trick is to make the grounded task's own initial state be the live world: edits are bit writes, thinks are searches from there, forks share the grounded tables by Arc. Everything is deterministic and thread-count independent: the same state, budget and goal give byte-identical plans at any threads.

Used by: the MCP session_* tools, the WASM WasmSession and its live pages, and the examples game_think, many_minds, bazaar_live, village_live.

children.title: session.rs: Session
children.summary: The ground-once embedding API: a grounded world plus one mind's private state. Edits rewrite the task's init; thinks are pure search from there. 3,623 lines, about 1,600 of them tests.
children.body:
ferroplan::solve re-parses and re-grounds on every call, and for small problems grounding dominates the wall clock. A game or agent runtime re-solving the same world every tick would pay that fixed cost for identical work. Session pays it once.

Representation. A Session owns a PackedTask whose operator tables are Arc-shared and whose initial state and goal are the mind's current belief and desire. So a world edit is a bit write into init_bits, a think is a search from task.initial(), and a fork is a refcount bump plus a copy of a few small vectors. Around the task sit immutable shared maps (fact/fluent/op names to ids, dynamic-fact table, mirror pairs, TIL setters) and per-mind fields (op mask, schedule, in-flight intervals, lifted goal).

Scope. Classical, numeric and ADL domains; temporal since 0.12; in-flight intervals and scheduled events since 0.14; budget-stamped orbit-aware thinks since 0.24. Rejected at construction: PDDL3 constraints and preferences (the metric optimizer compiles per solve) and absolute-clock TILs.

Honesty fences run through the whole API: statics and RUNNING-* tokens cannot be written, ADL goals cannot be retargeted, a capped think is never reported as unsolvable.

children.title: Session::new: ground once
children.summary: Parse, compile derived axioms, reject unsupported inputs, snap-compile if temporal, ground, then build the name maps, dynamic-fact table, mirror pairs and TIL setters that every later call relies on.
children.body:
Session::new (session.rs:340) is where the expensive work happens, once:

  1. Parse domain and problem; derived::compile folds static axioms.
  2. Reject PDDL3 trajectory constraints, preference problems and (for temporal domains) absolute-clock TILs, each with a message pointing to ferroplan::solve. Session time is always relative to now.
  3. Temporal domains: temporal::compile (snap actions) then ground_fixpoint. Classical: ground_task, which always returns a task even if the base goal is trivially true or false, because the world will move.
  4. Build fact_ids and fluent_ids (upper-case display to id), the dynamic table (any op or conditional effect adds or deletes it), op_ids, the RUNNING-* predicate list, and the bidirectional mirror map between (P ...) and (NOT (P ...)) facts.
  5. Temporal: append TIL setters. Classical: keep the lifted (Domain, Problem) in an Arc for per-think orbit detection.

Note on the struct: the current world state is not a separate field. It is the grounded task's own initial state (task.init_bits, fv0, fdef0) and goal (goal_pos, goal_num). Mutating the world means rewriting the task's init, and a think is just a search from task.initial().

children.title: Fixpoint grounding (temporal entry)
children.summary: Temporal sessions ground with ground_fixpoint: reached-restricted enumeration that costs what is reachable, not the typed product. elevator-11 p04: 31.6 s / 5.7 GB to 6.9 s / 48.8 MB, about 117x less transient memory.
children.body:
The idea. A naive grounder enumerates every type-correct binding of every action's parameters and discards those whose preconditions can never hold. That typed product can be enormous when most bindings are unreachable. Reached-restricted fixpoint grounding instead starts from the atoms true in init, and each round joins every action's positive dynamic top-level preconditions against the set of atoms reached so far, adding the effects of the new bindings to the reached set, until nothing changes. Bindings are deduped across rounds. Doomed candidates are never enumerated at all.

Numbers (docs/roadmap-0.12.md, Phase 3): elevator-11 p04, same binary A/B, 31.6 s / 5.7 GB to 6.9 s / 48.8 MB transient, identical task dimensions. The bazaar fixture shows the other side: 197k of 211k typed candidates are real ops, so fixpoint cannot help there, and the answer is simply to ground once at world load (5.5 s / 644 MB) and make every think pure search.

Why only the Session uses it. The surviving op set is identical, but fact ids are interned in a different first-reference order, so search tie-breaks shift. That cost sokoban-t real coverage (4/10 stratified vs 1/10 fixpoint), and a canonical-order pass could not recover it. So the corpus solve paths stay on stratified grounding, and the temporal Session, where the memory win matters and no scoreboard is disturbed, grounds via ground_fixpoint. Classical sessions use the plain ground_task. FF_NO_FIXPOINT_GROUND=1 falls back.

children.title: TIL setter ops behind a fence
children.summary: For temporal sessions, every dynamic fact gets two appended ops (TILSET-f, TILCLR-f) gated on a never-true TIL-NEVER fact, so scheduled events can be fired by the search's agenda without polluting the heuristic.
children.body:
append_til_setters (session.rs:228) runs once at construction for temporal sessions. It mints a fresh fact TIL-NEVER that is never true, then for every dynamic fact f appends two ops: TILSET-f (adds f, deletes its (NOT f) mirror) and TILCLR-f (the reverse). Each has TIL-NEVER as its only precondition.

The fence does the work. The relaxed planning graph and the search's own successor generation can never apply these ops, and they are deliberately not registered in add_by_fact, so they are never considered achievers. Only a pre-seeded agenda fires them, because Kind::Til events fire unconditionally: exogenous events do not ask permission. The result is a map (fact, value) -> op id that set_timed_fact uses to schedule events.

The function also rebuilds every derived index the growth invalidates: the CSR columns, shared_add, monitored, and the 0.27 successor index succ_by_fact. The comment is candid that a stale index was harmless only by luck, and "an invariant that is only true by luck is not an invariant."

children.title: World edits, observation, set_goal
children.summary: Edits write straight into the task's init bits and fluent arrays, behind fences: only dynamic facts, never RUNNING-* tokens, mirrors kept in sync. set_goal retargets without regrounding.
children.body:
set_fact(name, v) (session.rs:825) resolves the name through dynamic_fact_id, flips one bit in task.init_bits, and flips the mirror bit to !v if one exists. dynamic_fact_id enforces the fences: the fact must be grounded, must be dynamic, and must not be a compiler RUNNING-* token (atom_head looks through (NOT ...) so a mirror cannot dodge the fence).

Why statics are refused. Grounding enumerates operator parameters restricted by static predicates from init. Flipping a static after grounding could require operators that were never generated, so the session would return wrong plans silently. An error is the honest answer.

set_fluent (:1016) writes fv0[id] and marks it defined; all fluent values are read at runtime, so any grounded fluent may be set. observe(sight) (:844) validates the whole batch first, then updates only the sighted facts and returns those whose value differed from belief: the surprises. Facts outside the sight list keep their believed values, which is how fog is modeled.

set_goal(goal) (:1051) parses a ground conjunction (atoms, negated atoms with grounded mirrors, numeric comparisons) into goal_pos/goal_num over the existing fact space. ADL connectives error, since those compile at grounding time. Fluents a new numeric goal reads are added to the visited-key relevance closure, which only ever grows, so replay soundness and thread determinism hold across retargets. goal_met, fact and fluent are pure reads.

children.title: fork + restrict_ops: many minds
children.summary: fork() clones a mind over the same grounded world: PackedTask's columns are Arc-backed CSR, so a fork copies only state vectors. restrict_ops masks a mind to its own actions.
children.body:
fork (session.rs:596) builds a new Session with task.clone() and Arc::clone of every immutable map. This is cheap because PackedTask's operator tables are Csr<T> { flat: Arc<[T]>, off: Arc<[u32]> } and its name lists are Arc<[String]>: cloning bumps reference counts. What is actually copied is the per-mind state: init_bits, fv0, fdef0, goal_pos, goal_num, fluent relevance, plus the op mask, schedule and in-flight list.

The fork starts from the parent's current state and goal and then diverges with no shared tie-breaks. Measured on the vendored bazaar: 12 NPCs fork in about 0 ms with +0 MB RSS; benchmarks/bazaar-thinks.md records about 0.05 KB of private state per forked mind. world_bytes and mind_bytes (:1267, :1294) report the shared/private split as flat-byte floors.

restrict_ops(keep) (:576) builds a forbidden mask from op display names. It is the many-minds correctness primitive: a mind plans only its own actions, and a rival's moves reach it as set_fact drift, never as plan steps. The mask is an input to search, so determinism is unaffected, and a goal unreachable within the allowed ops is an honest solved: false. Loop-side policies such as claims compose on top by re-restricting before a think.

children.title: Thinking: replan, replan_budgeted, think
children.summary: Three entry points over two search arms. Each solves from the current world state toward the current goal, paying only search.
children.body: replan() (session.rs:1341) is unbounded beyond the session's max_evaluated. replan_budgeted(evals, mem) (:1334) is the real-time surface: an eval budget plus memory target, returning an honest solved: false when exhausted. think(&ThinkBudget) (:1797) is the 0.24 stamped contract. All three dispatch to a temporal arm when the session holds a TemporalCompiled, else to the classical ladder. All take &self: thinking never mutates the session, which is what lets the MCP server think on a fork without holding a lock.

children.title: Classical think: the search ladder
children.summary: replan_inner / think call search::plan_avoiding on the session's own task: EHC, then novelty-light, LAMA, novelty, then complete weighted best-first, with the mind's forbidden mask.
children.body:
For a classical session replan_inner (session.rs:1721) first short-circuits: if goal_met on the current state, return the empty plan. Otherwise it builds SearchCfg::from_weights(weight_g, weight_h, budget), sets node_bytes_target from memory_mb, and calls search::plan_avoiding(&self.task, threads, cfg, ehc_first, &self.forbidden, orbit).

plan_avoiding (search.rs:1733) is the same ladder solve uses for classical problems: enforced hill-climbing with helpful actions first (unless the session was opened with Search::BestFirst), then bounded rungs (novelty-light, the LAMA landmark rung, the novelty rung) when affordable, then weighted best-first as the complete fallback. The only differences from a one-shot solve are that the task is already grounded and its init is the live world, and that the forbidden mask is enforced inside successor generation.

max_evaluated is the deterministic budget: identical budgets give identical plans at any thread count. memory_mb becomes a byte target that the search converts to a node cap via its per-node byte model (node_cap_for_bytes).

children.title: Temporal think: seeded epoch ladder
children.summary: replan_temporal rebuilds the duration table against current fluents, merges scheduled events and running-interval ends into a root agenda, and runs the bounded decision-epoch ladder from the current state.
children.body:
replan_temporal (session.rs:628): only an at-rest world (no running intervals) takes the trivial goal-met exit, because a pending end could still unmeet the goal. Then temporal::build_kind reclassifies every op as Start/End/Classical against the current fluent values, so a set_fluent on a fluent no op modifies still flows into parameter-dependent durations.

The root agenda is built from self.timed (mapped through the TIL setter ops) plus self.running (real end ops), sorted by time then op id. temporal::solve_from_seeded_deadline then runs the decision-epoch ladder from task.initial(), with the mind's forbidden mask, the demand tier read once at construction, the eval budget spanning the whole ladder, and a node byte cap (default NODE_CAP_TARGET_BYTES, 8 GiB on 64-bit). Pending events also seed the heuristic, so plans can wait through an outage whose repair is scheduled. A returned plan is valid through every running interval: the goal only counts once no end is pending.

No escalation, no decomposer: "a think is a bounded call, not a campaign."

children.title: Think, ThinkBudget, ThinkVerdict
children.summary: think(&ThinkBudget) returns a Think: the Solution plus capped, spent_ms, spent_evals and a typed verdict (Solved, Capped, Exhausted). A cap never reads as unsolvable.
children.body:
ThinkBudget (session.rs:102) has three optional axes: max_evaluated (the deterministic unit), wall_ms (a per-think wall, machine-dependent, so pair it with evals when replay matters), memory_mb. Missing means session default, no wall, or the default byte model.

ThinkVerdict (:115) encodes the capped-vs-proven distinction in the type: Solved; Capped (no plan and some cap may have truncated the search, so the goal was not proven unreachable); Exhausted (no plan and the classical complete search genuinely ran out: unreachable within this mind's ops). Temporal thinks never return Exhausted, because the bounded decision-epoch ladder is incomplete on required-concurrency shapes and proves nothing by failing.

Session::think (:1797) sets cfg.deadline from wall_ms (the clock is checked at batch cadence), arms orbit canonicalization, and maps o.capped to the verdict, writing an explanatory note either way. The temporal arm (think_temporal, :1912) checks the wall only at pass boundaries and says so in a note. replan() and replan_budgeted() remain the older unstamped, orbit-free surface, unchanged byte for byte.

children.title: orbit_now: symmetry per think
children.summary: Classical, unrestricted thinks re-detect object symmetries on the current world and goal every call, never cached across edits; the canonical keys ride the best-first fallback.
children.body:
The idea. If two objects are interchangeable (same type, same static relations, symmetric in init and goal), states that differ only by swapping them are equivalent, and search can store one canonical representative. That prunes duplicate work on symmetric problems.

Why per think. A symmetry certified against the problem's init stops being valid the moment set_fact moves the world or set_goal changes what the mind wants. So orbit_now (session.rs:1970) rebuilds a lifted problem from the live state: static init atoms verbatim, dynamic facts and fluents re-read from the current tables, the goal from goal_formula. Then it calls orbits::detect_classical again. Detection is paid per think; nothing is cached.

Returns None for temporal sessions (their appended TIL-setter ops are outside any symmetry certification) and for restricted minds (to skip the detection cost, since a forbidden mask is caller-shaped). Only think uses it; replan and replan_following stay orbit-free.

children.title: Follow before you rethink
children.summary: plan_still_valid replays a plan's remaining suffix against the current state at zero search cost; replan_following keeps the surviving prefix and searches only a new tail.
children.body:
plan_still_valid(plan, from_step) (session.rs:737) answers whether the rest of a plan still executes from the current world and ends in the goal. Classical suffixes replay op by op (applicability plus effects, honoring the forbidden mask). Temporal suffixes replay their timed happenings in epoch order using the internal validator, including scheduled events and running ends. No search, no budget. An agent whose world drifted irrelevantly keeps following its plan for free.

replan_following(prior, from_step, evals, mem) (:1366) addresses dithering: an unconstrained rethink after a small break can return a structurally different plan, which looks like an NPC changing its mind for no reason. It replays the still-applicable prefix of the old suffix (cutting early if the goal is met along it), then seeds a task clone with the prefix's end state and searches only for a tail with plan_avoiding. If no tail exists it falls back to an unbiased replan_inner with the same budget and adds both eval counts. Measured: a deep break re-plans in 3 evals with churn 1, where an unbiased rethink spent 2,899 evals and churned 16 steps.

The temporal arm (replan_following_temporal, :1493) replays happenings to a simulated in-flight state, carries intervals whose ends lie past the break into the tail think as its root agenda, and shifts tail times by the break moment.

children.title: Scheduled world + in-flight intervals
children.summary: set_timed_fact schedules clock-relative fact flips; apply_start begins a durative action now; elapse(dt) fires due events and interval ends in time order and reports broken ends.
children.body:
Temporal sessions keep two schedules, both relative to now: timed: Vec<(dt, fact, value)> and running: Vec<(remaining, end_op)>.

set_timed_fact(dt, name, v) (session.rs:919) passes the same writability fences as set_fact and adds an event ("the market closes in five"). Every later think and validity replay sees it as a scheduled happening.

apply_start(name) (:495) applies a durative start's effects now, including the compiler's RUNNING-* token, and adds its end to running with a duration resolved against current fluents. It errors on classical sessions, unknown actions, and inapplicable starts. From then on a mind can rethink mid-interval: the end rides into thinks as a real happening and plans stay valid through it.

elapse(dt) (:952) splits both lists into due and remaining, decays the remaining times by dt, sorts the due items by time, and fires them: events write the fact bit and its mirror; ends apply the end op if its preconditions hold. Ends whose preconditions drift broke are returned by name with their effects dropped; the game decides what a ruined firing means. This retired the earlier idiom of mirroring end effects by hand with set_fact.

children.title: One game tick
children.summary: The loop every embedding runs: world moves, check goal, replay plan, rethink only if broken, act, advance time.
children.body: The native examples bazaar_live.rs and village_live.rs and their browser twins drive this loop. Most ticks stop at step 3 with a successful replay and spend no search at all.

children.title: 1. The world moves
children.summary: The game writes authoritative changes into the world session (set_fact / set_fluent) and each mind learns what it can see (observe, returning surprises).
children.body:
At the top of a tick the game applies what happened since last tick: its own effects, rivals' completed actions. In the bazaar each executed trade is written to the authoritative world and to the minds with set_fact (bazaar_live.rs:184). In fogged runs a mind instead calls observe(&sight) for the facts it can currently see (its own stall, its partner's on arrival) and gets back only the surprises (bazaar_live.rs:213). Unseen facts keep their believed values.

Cost: a few bit writes per fact. No grounding, no search.

children.title: 2. Am I done? goal_met
children.summary: A pure state test against the mind's current goal. If met, retire the goal or retarget with set_goal (zero regrounding).
children.body:
goal_met() evaluates the goal on task.initial(): no search, no budget. The doc comment stresses it is a different question from a zero-budget think, which asks whether a plan could still be found; near-done minds must not confuse the two.

If met, the game can retarget: the village re-hires a worker on its next contract via set_goal (village-live.html workerTurn), keeping the same grounded world.

children.title: 3. Still on plan? plan_still_valid
children.summary: Replay the remaining suffix from the mind's cursor. True means keep following, for free; false means drift broke it.
children.body:
The mind holds its last plan and a cursor. plan_still_valid(plan, cursor) replays the suffix exactly. In the serial bazaar loop a mind's suffix validated when it last acted, so any break found now was caused by rival actions in between, and is counted once as a conflict (bazaar_live.rs:249). The village does the same check on a probe fork with the worker's contract set.

This step is why most ticks cost almost nothing: thinking is surprise-driven, not scheduled.

children.title: 4. Rethink (only if broken)
children.summary: Re-scope the mind (restrict_ops, e.g. with claims), then a bounded think: replan_budgeted, replan_following, or the stamped think.
children.body:
Before thinking, the loop may refresh the mind's op mask: the claims policy masks trades that would take an item a rival's active plan still claims (bazaar_live.rs:307). Then a bounded think: replan_following(p, cursor, THINK_EVALS, Some(THINK_MB)) under the follow policy, else replan_budgeted(THINK_EVALS, Some(THINK_MB)) (bazaar_live.rs:318), with THINK_EVALS = 20_000 and THINK_MB = 128. MCP callers use session_replan, which is think.

This is the only step that searches, and it reuses the grounding from construction: the search runs on the session's own PackedTask whose init is the live state. A capped or failed think is a normal outcome: the mind waits and retries next tick.

children.title: 5. Act: apply the next step
children.summary: Classical worlds apply the step's effects with set_fact on the world; temporal worlds dispatch due steps with apply_start.
children.body: Classical: the game applies the next step's effects to the authoritative world (and the acting mind), advancing the cursor (bazaar_live.rs:439). Temporal: the village loop walks plan steps whose start time has come and calls world.apply_start("(ACTION ARGS)"); a start that is not yet applicable stays queued for the next tick (village_live.rs:172, village-live.html dispatch).

children.title: 6. Advance time: elapse
children.summary: Temporal worlds call elapse(dt): due scheduled events and interval ends fire in time order; broken ends are reported.
children.body:
The village advances one time unit per tick with world.elapse(1.0) (village_live.rs:99). Interval ends whose time has come apply their at-end effects; events planted with set_timed_fact flip their facts. Anything that changed here becomes the drift the next tick's step 3 checks for.

Determinism: with budgeted thinks and a fixed mind order the whole simulation replays byte-identical at any thread count, which the session tests assert (*_stay_deterministic_across_threads).

children.title: Session vs solve: what is reused
children.summary: Paid once at Session::new: parse, axiom compile, snap compile, grounding, index building. Paid per think: one search (plus duration rebuild for temporal, orbit detection for stamped classical thinks).
